# Methodology {#sec-methodology}

```{python}
#| label: methodology-setup
from pathlib import Path

from ryuk.detector import MAX_DETECTION_SIDE, NMS_THRESHOLD, SCORE_THRESHOLD
from ryuk.eda.files import read_summary
from ryuk.evaluation.names import model_name
from ryuk.evaluation.results import read_results
from ryuk.recognition.arcface import ArcFace
from ryuk.recognition.facenet import FaceNet
from ryuk.recognition.sface import SFace

# Quarto runs the kernel in report/, so the committed outputs are one level up.
method_summary = read_summary(Path("../eda"))
method_results = read_results(Path("../evaluation/results.json"))
assert method_results is not None
method_lfw = {m.model.network: m for m in method_results.verification.models}
crop_trials = {t.crop: t for t in method_results.verification.view_1 if t.network == "facenet"}
chosen_crop = next(t.crop for t in crop_trials.values() if t.chosen)
int8 = method_results.verification.sface_int8
on_rule = {
    rule: [model_name(t.model) for t in method_results.thresholds if t.rule == rule]
    for rule in ("best-photo", "mean")
}
# The prose names these; stop the render if the results say otherwise.
assert method_lfw["sface"].crop == method_lfw["arcface"].crop == "five-point"
assert method_lfw["facenet"].crop == chosen_crop == "box-margin-32"
assert set(crop_trials) == {"five-point", "box-margin-14", "box-margin-32"}
assert len(on_rule["best-photo"]) == 1 and len(on_rule["mean"]) == 2
assert int8.ms_per_face_int8 > int8.ms_per_face_fp32


def margin(crop: str) -> str:
    return crop.rsplit("-", 1)[1]


def dev_test(crop: str) -> str:
    return f"{100 * crop_trials[crop].accuracy:.2f}%"
```

## Pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

Every face Ryuk scores, in evaluation, at enrollment and in the live monitor, goes through one pipeline. YuNet finds each face and gives its box and five landmarks, the eyes, the tip of the nose and the corners of the mouth, at its default face score threshold of `{python} f"{SCORE_THRESHOLD:g}"` and non-maximum suppression threshold of `{python} f"{NMS_THRESHOLD:g}"`. Only a usable face goes further: one whose box's short side is at least the minimum usable face size, `{python} method_summary.min_usable_face_size.value` px, which @sec-data-detection fixed from CelebA's detections. A smaller detection is shown in the live monitor as too small, ignored at enrollment and excluded from evaluation. YuNet misses a face that fills a large image, so live frames and uploaded photos are detected on a copy whose long side is at most `{python} MAX_DETECTION_SIDE` px, and the boxes are scaled back; benchmark images are smaller than that and are detected as they are.

Each usable face is then cut out in the form its recognition model takes. For SFace and ArcFace that is OpenCV's `alignCrop`, which maps the five landmarks onto ArcFace's template in a `{python} SFace.input_size`-pixel square. FaceNet takes a `{python} FaceNet.input_size`-pixel crop of YuNet's box widened by a margin, the crop its View 1 trial chose (@sec-models). The model turns the crop into one embedding, which is L2-normalised and kept as float32, so the cosine of two embeddings is their dot product.

A face is compared with a person of interest through a match score, computed from the face's embedding and the person's enrolled embeddings under the recognition model's live rule. The baseline rule, best photo, is the cosine to the person's most similar enrolled photo. The learning comparison of @sec-eval-learning put a second rule live for two models: the mean rule, the cosine to the renormalised mean of the person's enrolled embeddings, scores faces for `{python} " and ".join(on_rule["mean"])`, and `{python} on_rule["best-photo"][0]` keeps best photo. The person with the highest match score is the top candidate, and the face is a match when that score is at or above the model's threshold. The search is exact: the active model's embeddings of everyone on the watchlist are held in one matrix in memory, and a face is scored against all of them with one matrix product. At a watchlist's size that costs microseconds against the milliseconds of detection and embedding, so there is no approximate index.

A benchmark image contributes one face, its centre-most usable face: of its usable detections, the one whose box centre is nearest the image centre (@sec-data-detection). An image with none is excluded before any recognition model runs, so every model is measured on the same faces. A live frame contributes every usable face, each scored on its own, and an enrolled photo must hold exactly one.

## Recognition models {#sec-models}

Ryuk compares three recognition models, all pretrained, open source and frozen: none is trained or fine-tuned here (ADR 0002). SFace is the OpenCV zoo's model, run in fp32 through OpenCV's DNN module, and gives `{python} method_lfw["sface"].model.dimension`-dimensional embeddings from `{python} SFace.input_size`-pixel faces. ArcFace is InsightFace's `w600k_r50`, a ResNet-50 from the buffalo_l pack, run on onnxruntime: on Apple Silicon through the CoreML execution provider in its MLProgram format, whose embeddings match the CPU's (#7), and on the CPU elsewhere. It gives `{python} method_lfw["arcface"].model.dimension` dimensions from `{python} ArcFace.input_size`-pixel faces. FaceNet is facenet-pytorch's Inception-ResNet-v1 trained on VGGFace2, run on the CPU, and gives `{python} method_lfw["facenet"].model.dimension` dimensions from `{python} FaceNet.input_size`-pixel faces.

A recognition model is more than its network. Ryuk identifies one by its network, the sha256 of the weights file it loaded, the execution provider it runs on and the crop that cuts its faces, and a change to any of them makes a different recognition model. Embeddings from different recognition models are never compared: each model has its own threshold, every enrolled photo is embedded under each (@sec-storage), and a sighting records the model that produced it. ArcFace on CoreML and ArcFace on the CPU are therefore two recognition models, and the committed results, measured on an Apple Silicon Mac, give the second no threshold (@sec-reproducing).

SFace also ships quantised to int8, the form crimdet used. It is measured, but as a footnote to @tbl-lfw rather than as a fourth model. On the machine the results were measured on it took `{python} f"{int8.ms_per_face_int8:.1f}"` ms to embed a face against fp32's `{python} f"{int8.ms_per_face_fp32:.1f}"` ms, so it is slower, and its embeddings drift from fp32's: their cosine to the fp32 embeddings of the same `{python} f"{int8.faces_compared:,}"` faces is `{python} f"{int8.cosine_to_fp32_mean:.3f}"` on average and `{python} f"{int8.cosine_to_fp32_min:.3f}"` at worst. It is built for memory-constrained, integer-accelerated hardware, which an Apple Silicon Mac is not.

Pipeline choices are made on LFW View 1, never on View 2 or CelebA: a candidate's threshold is set on `pairsDevTrain` and its accuracy measured on `pairsDevTest`. The only such choice is FaceNet's crop, between the five-point alignment SFace and ArcFace use and YuNet's box widened by a margin of `{python} margin("box-margin-14")` or `{python} margin("box-margin-32")` pixels: facenet-pytorch's default margin, and the margin FaceNet's published figure was measured with. On `pairsDevTest` the five-point crop scored `{python} dev_test("five-point")`, margin `{python} margin("box-margin-14")` `{python} dev_test("box-margin-14")` and margin `{python} margin("box-margin-32")` `{python} dev_test("box-margin-32")`, and margin `{python} margin(chosen_crop)` was chosen. The choice has one exception on record. Margin `{python} margin("box-margin-32")` became a candidate only after FaceNet's first View 2 run, with margin `{python} margin("box-margin-14")`, was flagged against its published figure, so View 2 was not unseen when the candidates were set, and FaceNet's View 2 was scored twice (@sec-eval-lfw).

## Evaluation protocol {#sec-protocol}

```{python}
#| label: protocol-setup
from ryuk.evaluation.active import MAX_MS_PER_FACE, MAX_TEST_FPIR
from ryuk.evaluation.bootstrap import DISAGREEMENT, WILSON_BELOW
from ryuk.evaluation.draws import (
    ENROLLED_PER_IDENTITY,
    GALLERY_SIZE,
    MATED_PROBES_PER_IDENTITY,
    MIN_GALLERY_IMAGES,
    NON_MATED_PROBES_PER_IDENTITY,
)

protocol = method_results
assert protocol.identification is not None and protocol.first_active_model is not None
assert protocol.learning is not None and protocol.bias is not None and protocol.live is not None
# The prose counts the methods; stop the render if the results say otherwise.
assert all(len(c.methods) == 6 for c in protocol.learning.models)
protocol_lfw = protocol.verification
protocol_gate = protocol.first_active_model.lfw_gate
protocol_points = protocol_lfw.models[0].operating_points
assert [p.indicative for p in protocol_points] == [False, True]
# Every model is read at the same operating points, and the same intervals.
assert all(
    [p.target_far for p in m.operating_points] == [p.target_far for p in protocol_points]
    for m in protocol_lfw.models
)
protocol_ids = protocol.identification
protocol_fpir = protocol_ids.models[0].target_fpir
indicative_fpir = next(p.target_fpir for p in protocol_ids.models[0].test.operating_points if p.indicative)
assert all(m.target_fpir == protocol_fpir for m in protocol_ids.models)
# Mismatched pairs are half of View 2's, so about half of those scored.
mismatched = protocol_gate.scored_pairs / 2


def share(value: float) -> str:
    return f"{100 * value:g}%"
```

Ryuk measures each recognition model twice, on two questions: verification on LFW, whether two faces are the same person, and open-set identification on CelebA, whose face this is, if anyone's on the watchlist. The protocol was fixed before the test draw was scored (#9), and everything in it is applied by the code that wrote the committed results.

### Verification {#sec-protocol-verification}

LFW View 2 checks that each recognition model runs as its authors published it. Its `{python} f"{protocol_lfw.pairs:,}"` pairs fall into `{python} len(protocol_lfw.models[0].folds)` folds, each with equal numbers of matched and mismatched pairs, and Ryuk scores them by the ten-fold recipe the OpenCV zoo and InsightFace publish their figures with. A pair's score is the cosine of its two embeddings; each fold's threshold is the one that scores best on the other nine, over InsightFace's grid; and accuracy is the mean over the folds, ± the standard error LFW defines, the folds' standard deviation over the square root of their number. A pair is scored only when both its images have a usable face (@sec-eval-lfw).

AUC, and TAR at FAR `{python} share(protocol_points[0].target_far)` and `{python} share(protocol_points[1].target_far)`, are read from every scored pair pooled, a pair being accepted at or above a threshold as the live monitor accepts a match. Their thresholds are read off the same pairs, so they are in-sample. TAR at FAR `{python} share(protocol_points[1].target_far)` is indicative only: about `{python} f"{round(mismatched, -2):,.0f}"` mismatched pairs allow about `{python} round(mismatched * protocol_points[1].target_far)` false accepts at that rate.

### Watchlist search {#sec-protocol-identification}

Open-set identification rehearses the watchlist on CelebA in two draws: the validation draw is CelebA's `valid` split and the test draw its `test` split, and the two share no identities. Images with no usable face are excluded first. In each draw `{python} GALLERY_SIZE` identities with at least `{python} MIN_GALLERY_IMAGES` usable images are drawn at random, with a fixed seed, into the gallery, each with `{python} ENROLLED_PER_IDENTITY` enrolled photos and exactly `{python} MATED_PROBES_PER_IDENTITY` mated probes. Every other identity with a usable image is held out, with up to `{python} NON_MATED_PROBES_PER_IDENTITY` of its images as non-mated probes, the evaluation's stand-in for strangers. TPIR is the share of mated probes whose top candidate is their own identity and scores at or above the threshold; misidentification is the share whose top candidate is another identity and scores at or above it; FPIR is the share of non-mated probes matched to anyone. Rank-1, the share of mated probes whose top candidate is their own identity whatever its score, is reported beside them.

Each recognition model's threshold is the lowest match score at which FPIR on the validation draw is at or below `{python} share(protocol_fpir)`. It is frozen there, and only then is the test draw scored, once, at that threshold. The code enforces the order: a threshold can be frozen only from the validation draw's scores, and the test draw can be scored only at a frozen threshold. TPIR at FPIR `{python} share(indicative_fpir)`, read off each model's own test curve, is reported as indicative: at that rate the test draw's `{python} f"{protocol_ids.selection('test').non_mated_probes:,}"` non-mated probes allow about `{python} round(protocol_ids.selection('test').non_mated_probes * indicative_fpir)` false alarms.

### Confidence intervals {#sec-protocol-intervals}

Every CelebA rate carries a `{python} share(protocol_ids.bootstrap.confidence)` identity-level percentile bootstrap interval from `{python} f"{protocol_ids.bootstrap.resamples:,}"` resamples with a fixed seed. Identities are resampled with replacement, never single probes, because one person's probes resemble one another and are not independent; gallery and held-out identities are resampled separately. A bootstrap interval can under-cover a rate near 0 or 100%, so every error rate below `{python} share(WILSON_BELOW)`, and every success rate above `{python} share(1 - WILSON_BELOW)`, is also given a dependence-adjusted Wilson interval (@sec-protocol-wilson).

### The first active model {#sec-protocol-active}

The live monitor starts with the first active model, chosen by a rule. A recognition model is eligible if it reproduces its published LFW accuracy within `{python} f"{protocol_gate.tolerance_points:g}"` points over the pairs it scored, keeps test FPIR at its frozen threshold at or below `{python} share(MAX_TEST_FPIR)`, and takes at most `{python} f"{MAX_MS_PER_FACE:g}"` ms per face from pixels to top candidate. That time is the median over a sample of the test draw's probes on the machine the results were measured on, detection included. CelebA's images are smaller than a webcam frame, so detecting the faces in a live frame can take longer than it did there. Among eligible models the one with the highest test TPIR at its frozen threshold wins, unless another eligible model's interval overlaps it, in which case the fastest of those wins instead. Each model is judged under the rule it runs live. The operator can switch to any other recognition model with a measured threshold.

### Learning and bias {#sec-protocol-learning}

Two further experiments reuse the CelebA draws and their intervals. The learning comparison (@sec-eval-learning) scores six methods on each recognition model: the best-photo and mean scoring rules, three classifiers trained on the gallery's enrolled embeddings, and the learned decision rule. Every fitted choice is made on the validation draw only: each classifier's hyperparameter, the learned rule's coefficients, whose cut-off is frozen on out-of-fold output from `{python} protocol.learning.folds`-fold identity-grouped cross-fitting, and every threshold. Methods are compared by TPIR at FPIR `{python} share(protocol.learning.target_fpir)` on the test draw. A method improves on best photo only if the `{python} share(protocol.learning.bootstrap.confidence)` paired identity-level bootstrap interval of its gain lies wholly above zero, both methods being read in the same resamples, and only a method that needs no retraining when the watchlist changes can go live. The bias breakdown (@sec-eval-bias) reports TPIR, misidentification and FPIR per group on the test draw at each model's single frozen threshold. Male and Young group identities by majority label, with at least `{python} share(protocol.bias.agreement)` of an identity's images agreeing; Eyeglasses, Wearing_Hat and Blurry group probes by their own label; and no rate is estimated from fewer than `{python} protocol.bias.min_identities` identities.

### Away from the rehearsal {#sec-protocol-live}

Two last measurements reuse the same draws to ask what the rehearsal does not (@sec-eval-live). Each recognition model's same-person threshold, the one-to-one cut-off of the warning that a photo added to a person of interest may not be them, is frozen at a false-accept rate of `{python} share(protocol.live.models[0].same_person.target_far)` on the validation draw's impostor pairs with one enrolled photo, read off the curve by the same rule as the one-to-many threshold; the test draw then reports the false-accept rate and the share of a person's own photos that would warn, with one photo enrolled and with every one. And the test draw's gallery is split at random into smaller disjoint watchlists, each scored under the model's live rule at its frozen threshold, with every enrolled photo and with one. Neither changes the threshold the live monitor matches faces at.

### The adjusted Wilson interval {#sec-protocol-wilson}

The identity-level bootstrap can under-cover a rate near 0 or 100% (Fogliato et al.), and on a rate of exactly 0 it collapses altogether: every resample of a group with no errors has none. Every error rate below `{python} share(WILSON_BELOW)`, and every success rate above `{python} share(1 - WILSON_BELOW)`, therefore also gets Wilson's interval with the number of trials replaced by an effective sample size that allows for one identity's probes being alike, Fogliato et al.'s recommendation R1:

$$N^* = \min\left(\max\left(\frac{p(1-p)}{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(p)},\ G\right),\ N\right), \qquad \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(p) = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{g=1}^{G} (e_g - p\,n_g)^2,$$

where $p$ is the rate, $N$ the number of trials, $G$ the number of identities behind them, and $e_g$ and $n_g$ identity $g$'s errors and trials. The floor at $G$ is Fogliato et al.'s for a rate whose trials are clustered by one identity, and it is what $N^*$ becomes when the variance is 0, as it is for a rate of exactly 0. The cap at $N$ is Ryuk's, not theirs. As the variance nears 0 without reaching it, $N^*$ grows without bound, and identities more alike than independent trials would make the adjusted interval narrower than the textbook Wilson interval. Capped, the adjustment only ever widens it. Where the adjusted interval differs meaningfully from the bootstrap, meaning an end moves by more than `{python} share(DISAGREEMENT)` of the wider interval's width, the report gives both.
